analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid painkiller makers a penny per milligram to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was referred there on May 24, 2016 and no vote was ever held before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a one-cent-per-milligram excise tax on opioid pain relievers at the point they are made or imported, with exemptions for addiction-treatment medications. Cancer and hospice patients would be rebated or discounted so they bear none of the tax. Whatever revenue remains after those protections would flow to states through the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant, earmarked exclusively for building treatment facilities, sober living homes, residential programs, and care for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome. The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: People struggling with opioid addiction and their communities: states would gain dedicated federal funding to build new treatment facilities, expand residential and outpatient programs, recruit providers in underserved areas, and care for infants born dependent on opioids. Cancer and hospice patients who legitimately need opioids would be protected by a rebate or discount program so the tax does not raise their costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with opioid addiction and their communities

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on opioid pain relievers sold by manufacturers, producers, or importers, exempting drugs used exclusively to treat opioid addiction.
Requires HHS to rebate or discount the tax for cancer and hospice patients so they face no economic burden from it.

Directs any net revenue from the tax to states under the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant, exclusively for substance abuse treatment efforts including new treatment facilities, sober living housing, long-term residential programs, and facilities for babies with neonatal abstinence syndrome.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers pay the tax directly. If manufacturers pass the cost through, retail prices could rise for pain patients outside the protected groups — the bill itself orders a report on exactly that risk — and patients whose opioid use is not tied to cancer or hospice care get no rebate protection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid manufacturers; possibly other pain patients

drawbacks.text: The tax could raise the retail cost of opioid pain relievers for patients outside the cancer and hospice rebate program, and the bill requires an HHS report on the impact on retail prices and patient access — an acknowledgment that the mechanism carries that risk.

Funding for treatment depends entirely on the net revenue the tax raises each year, so the new programs are only as well-funded as opioid sales and the revenue after patient rebates allow; there is no guaranteed appropriation.
An excise tax on legitimate pain medicine adds a new cost layer to prescribing, which critics of such taxes argue can make access harder for chronic pain patients even as it targets overproduction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is substantial: a permanent, dedicated funding stream for addiction treatment during the opioid epidemic, with the strongest cost protections built in for the patients with the clearest medical need. The main costs fall on opioid manufacturers, with a residual risk of higher retail prices for non-protected pain patients. On balance, the design is careful — the treatment mandate and patient rebates are specific and enforceable — but the revenue-based funding is inherently uncertain, and honest supporters would concede the tax touches legitimate pain treatment as well as the epidemic it targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Joe Manchin introduced the bill on May 24, 2016 with an initial group of senators including Klobuchar, Shaheen, King, Heitkamp, Baldwin, Nelson, Warren, Schatz, and Heinrich.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill gathered 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no committee action, markup, or floor vote followed, and the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off: the per-milligram excise tax never took effect and no treatment funding stream was created, leaving states to pay for addiction treatment as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who avoided the tax

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin III
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia (lead sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial group of nine co-introducing senators.

for.name: Sen. Angus King
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maine (Independent, caucuses with Democrats)

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Angus King; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would charge them one cent per milligram of active opioid sold, a direct per-unit cost on their core pain-relief products. Their interest in blocking it ran against the bill's public health purpose of funding addiction treatment.

industries.industry: Substance abuse treatment providers and facilities
industries.note: New state block grant money would fund addiction treatment facilities, residential and outpatient programs, sober living housing, and care for infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome. Their gain is the public's gain: more treatment capacity.

The bill singles out their patients for full rebate or discount protection from the tax, so they are largely shielded, though any pass-through pricing could add friction at the pharmacy counter until rebates are processed.
